..
Issued at 1248 AM CST Wed Nov 25 2026

Recent GOES-19 water vapor imagery depicts a pair of upper- 
level shortwaves meandering across the central US: One diving 
southeastward near the Missouri River and another propagating 
eastward across the ArkLaTex region. Expansive upper-level 
cirrus clouds extend between both waves and through the central 
Great lakes. Closer to the surface, a large west-to-east 
elongated high pressure system is centered across the 
northeastern United States, with the westward extension reaching
as far back as the Mississippi River. Initial surface low 
development associated with the upper-level troughs is already 
underway over the northern Gulf. Over the next few days, the 
aforementioned upper-level waves are expected to interact and 
eventually phase leading to the development of a large low 
pressure system over the eastern United States. Model guidance 
has come into better agreement with the exact phasing evolution 
and track in the storm system, leading to increasing forecast 
confidence locally.

Today into tonight, the northern-stream trough will drop 
southward toward the Missouri/Arkansas border while the 
southern-stream wave shifts eastward along the Gulf Coast. 
Increasing easterly low- to mid-level warm air advection on the
east and northern sides of the systems, respectively, will lead
to the development of a north-to-south oriented band of 
precipitation near or just east of the Mississippi River, 
southwest of our area. (This initial band of precipitation is
poised to verify on the very far southwestern side of the 
ensemble envelope from a few days ago). While a few sprinkles or
flurries cannot be ruled out west of I-55 and south of I-80 on 
the northeastern fringe of the precipitation band today, the 
majority of our area will remain dry. Overcast skies and 
blustery easterly winds will nevertheless make it feel chilly 
with highs only expected to reach around 40 degrees.

Tonight, the phasing process will begin between the two waves 
leading to the rapid strengthening and north-northwestward 
movement of a surface low pressure system from the Carolina coast
toward the central Appalachian Mountains. A broad and 
intensifying region of upper-level diffluence within the merging
waves will facilitate the rapid expansion of an elongated west-
to-east oriented deformation band over the Ohio River Valley. A
steady feed of dry air into the Lower Great Lakes on the 
southern side of a retreating high pressure system should impede
the northward progress of the rain shield overnight, leading to
a dry night in our area. Continued northeasterly winds (onshore
flow) and overcast skies will lead to a muted diurnal 
temperature drop tonight with overnight lows favored to stay in 
the mid to upper 30s. 

Tomorrow, the two upper-level waves will fully consolidate 
pulling the surface low northward toward Lake Erie. A 
formidable northwestward push of the warm conveyer belt and 
associated column moisture in the mature cyclone during the 
afternoon hours should allow for an associated northward push of
the deformation band. There remains spread in the ensemble 
envelope on the exact track of the surface low, leading to 
spread on the northwestern edge of the precipitation shield. At 
this point, our forecast favors the northwestern edge making it 
to I-55 by Thursday evening with lower confidence with westward 
extent (it may remain completely dry west of I-39). Steady rain 
will then continue within the deformation band through the 
overnight hours before tapering quickly from west to east toward
daybreak Friday. 

Am noting an increasing signal for strong northeasterly winds 
Thursday afternoon and evening as cold-air advection commences 
within the tightening low-level pressure gradient between a 
1030mb surface high extension over Lake Superior and the 
sub-1000mb low lifting toward Lake Erie. Forecast BUFKIT 
profiles from both the RRFS and GFS would support frequent gusts
of 30 to 40 mph with locally higher gusts along the immediate 
Lake Michigan shoreline. Such gusts are easily supported by the 
EPS, but will note GEFS output is far less bullish. Will go 
ahead and increase winds in the gridded database and allow later
shifts to make refinements. 

Taken together, Thursday evening is shaping up to be rather raw
across northeastern Illinois and northwestern Indiana. With 
that said, what once looked like a complete washout for our area
Wednesday night into Thursday has trended decidedly better for 
a good chunk of our forecast area. Parts of northwestern 
Illinois (Rockford) may not see a drop of rain through this 
entire event. Perhaps even the west and northern Chicago
metropolitan area may remain completely dry should members on 
the eastern side of the ensemble envelope verify. The trend is
our friend! 


Friday into the weekend: 

Any lingering showers on Friday should end by early afternoon 
as upper-level short-wavelength ridging slides into the Great 
Lakes.
